questions.stem: Sylvie, 23, has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 86 g/L) from heavy menstrual bleeding and is starting treatment in general practice. You are safety netting before she leaves. Which bleeding pattern should you tell her means she needs to go to the emergency department?
options: Passing clots larger than a 50-cent coin on the first day of a period
A period that lasts longer than 7 days
Soaking a pad or tampon every hour for 2 hours or more
Needing to get up overnight to change pads or tampons
questions.why: Soaking a pad or tampon every hour for 2 hours or more (or heavy bleeding with dizziness or fainting) means acute heavy loss and needs urgent review in ED. The other features show chronic heavy menstrual bleeding and are managed in general practice.
notes: Large clots are a marker of heavy menstrual bleeding, which she already has, but they do not on their own mean acute, dangerous loss.
Periods longer than 7 days suggest heavy menstrual bleeding (hers last 8 days), but this is the chronic problem being treated, not an emergency.
Overnight changes help define heavy menstrual bleeding in the history, but she already does this, so it cannot be her trigger to go to ED.

questions.stem: Sylvie, 23, has Hb 86 g/L, MCV 68 fL, ferritin 4 µg/L and a normal CRP. Resting HR is 104 with a small postural drop, but she has no chest pain, no syncope and no active heavy bleeding. She has never taken iron. Which is the most appropriate first-line iron replacement?
options: Oral iron, about 100 mg elemental iron daily or on alternate days
IV ferric carboxymaltose infusion this week, because her Hb is below 90 g/L
Red cell transfusion of 1 unit, then oral iron
questions.why: Oral iron (about 100 mg elemental daily or on alternate days, with vitamin C and away from tea, coffee and dairy) is first line in a stable patient. IV iron is kept for intolerance, failure, malabsorption or when a rapid rise is needed.
notes: An Hb below 90 g/L is not on its own a reason for IV iron; it is used when oral iron fails, is not tolerated or is not absorbed, or when a rapid rise is needed.
Transfusion is not needed for a stable patient with chronic iron deficiency, and it exposes her to transfusion risks for no benefit.
IM iron is painful, can stain the skin permanently and is not recommended, now that oral and IV options are available.

questions.stem: Sylvie, 23, with ferritin 4 µg/L, is starting oral iron. Your GP supervisor suggests she take about 100 mg elemental iron on alternate days rather than daily, saying each dose may then be absorbed better and cause fewer side effects. What is the main mechanism behind this?
options: Daily doses keep gastric pH high, so less ferric iron is reduced to ferrous iron
Iron suppresses erythropoietin, so the marrow takes up less iron on dosing days
Unabsorbed iron injures duodenal villi, and a day off lets the mucosa recover
Each dose raises hepcidin, which breaks down ferroportin and cuts absorption next day
questions.why: An oral iron dose raises hepcidin for about 24 hours. Hepcidin binds ferroportin on enterocytes and causes it to be broken down, which blocks iron export. A dose taken the next day is therefore absorbed less well, and spacing doses lets hepcidin fall back.
notes: Iron does not raise gastric pH; acid (helped by vitamin C) supports reduction to ferrous iron, and this does not explain the benefit of alternate days.
Iron does not suppress erythropoietin, which is driven by tissue hypoxia, and her anaemia keeps EPO high.
Iron can irritate the GI tract and cause nausea, but villous injury is not the reason alternate-day dosing improves absorption.

questions.stem: Sylvie, 23, has heavy menstrual bleeding. Menstrual blood comes from spiral arterioles in the endometrial functional layer, fed by radial and arcuate arteries in the myometrium. Which vessel is the main arterial supply to the uterus?
options: Ovarian artery, arising directly from the abdominal aorta
Uterine artery, from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery
Internal pudendal artery, from the anterior division of the internal iliac
Uterine artery, from the posterior division of the internal iliac artery
questions.why: The uterine artery comes off the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. It crosses above the ureter ('water under the bridge') and joins the ovarian artery. This is the vessel targeted in uterine artery embolisation.
notes: The ovarian artery joins the uterine artery near the fundus but is not the main uterine supply. It mainly supplies the ovary and tube.
The internal pudendal artery supplies the perineum and external genitalia, not the uterus.
The posterior division of the internal iliac gives parietal branches (iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal), not the visceral uterine artery.
